title: Toronto police officer Const. David Cavanagh exonerated — again — in 2010 shooting of Eric Osawe
subtitle: The Ontario Court of Appeal has dismissed the Crown\'s attempt to overturn a judge\'s decision to toss a second-degree murder charge against Const. David Cavanagh
article: A Toronto police officer has been exonerated - again - in the Sept. 29, 2010 shooting of 26-year-old Eric Osawe.

Const. David Cavanagh, a member of the force\'s Emergency Task Force, was originally charged with manslaughter in Mr. Osawe\'s death, but the charge was later upped without explanation to second-degree murder by Ian Scott, then the director of the province\'s Special Investigations Unit, which probes all serious incidents involving police.

The Ontario Court of Appeal Wednesday dismissed a Crown appeal seeking to overturn the decision last year by Ontario Court Judge Michael Block, who tossed the murder charge at the end of a preliminary hearing and also concluded there was no evidence supporting even a manslaughter charge.

The only issue before the appeal court was the Crown allegation that Judge Block went too far and exceeded his jurisdiction by ruling there wasn\'t evidence of manslaughter. Crown lawyers wanted the constable to "be ordered to stand trial for manslaughter based on careless use of the firearm with his trigger off the trigger or on the trigger."
But as the appeal court drily put it, "The central problem for the appellant [the Crown] is that it adduced no evidence" showing that Const. Cavanagh had handled his weapon carelessly.
In fact, the appeal court noted, "the only evidence was that [Cavanagh] handled the firearm" in accordance both with force training and practice.

When the ETF made what\'s called a "dynamic" entry into Mr. Osawe\'s apartment on the night in question, it was with a search warrant, and that warrant, Judge Block said, was "grounded in an excellent credible basis for the belief that Mr. Osawe traded in cocaine and handguns... Indeed, cocaine and a loaded 9mm handgun were located in the Osawe apartment."
When the ETF burst in, they found his brother sitting in the living room and some officers stayed to control him.

Others, including Const. Cavanagh, entered the bedroom, where Mr. Osawe was lying on the bed. He refused the command to lie down on the floor, and during the ensuing struggle, was killed by a single shot from Const. Cavanagh\'s MP5 submachine gun.
Mr. Osawe had previously been convicted of a robbery and what Judge Block called "a knife-point home invasion involving a woman and a small child."

Still, the judge said, it wasn\'t Mr. Osawe\'s "serious criminal antecedents" which dictated that the ETF would batter down the door and use a flash bang distraction device, but rather his "current status as an armed drug and firearms trader."

The appeal court found that Judge Block "did not err in interpreting the evidence as showing the death of Mr. Osawe resulted from a \'tragic but accidental confluence of circumstances that occurred in a high-pressure and high-risk situation...\'"
As Judge Block wrote, "Until the moment of his death, Mr. Osawe continued to resist. The police were not subduing a shoplifter."
